column4: The seven heavens are layered without disparity in the Merciful's creation; this intact cosmic fitting is the direct opposite of the breach and overflow that the section carries into the soul.
Repeated sight returns unable to find a flaw in the heavens of 67:3, sharpening the contrast between cosmic order and a soul that tears its proper boundary.
The sky above is built and adorned "without any rifts"; its unbroken construction gives a specific cosmic boundary against which the section's rupture image can be seen.
The earth is spread, stabilized, and made to grow beautiful kinds, continuing the intact sky of 50:6 into the section's ordered and cultivated ground.
God builds heaven with power and expands it; this directly repeats the built-sky pole of the section's taswiya meeting.
God spreads the earth as an excellent preparer, completing the heaven-and-spread-earth pair begun in 51:47.
The earth is made a resting spread, a concise parallel to the section's laid-out ground between formation and destruction.
Mountains serve as pegs for the spread earth of 78:6, adding the stability that the later leveling scene removes.
God makes night a garment, directly joining the cosmic covering of night to the section's developed clothing sense of taqwa.
Day is made the time of livelihood, so the removal of night's garment yields provision in the ordered succession described by the section.
The oath by night "when it covers" repeats the exact opening action of surah 91 and begins another movement from cosmic alternation to unlike moral efforts.
The oath by day "when it manifests" supplies the answering uncovering to 92:1, matching the section's orderly opening after cover.
Your efforts are diverse carries the paired night and day of 92:1-2 into opposed human courses, the same cosmic-to-inward movement developed in the section.
The oath by morning brightness names the illuminated side of the dawn meeting, while 93:2 gives its nocturnal counterpart.
Night when it grows still supplies a peaceful form of covering beside 93:1, a boundary-preserving contrast to the section's inward overflow.
The sky splitting open at judgment turns the section's constructive sky into a breached one; it also prepares the seas' bursting in 82:3.
God turns to the smoke-like heaven and commands heaven and earth to come willingly, placing both structures under a single ordering command.
God completes the heavens as seven and assigns each its command, continuing 41:11 with the precise cosmic fitting that the section transfers to the soul.
God creates heavens and earth, sends water, brings fruit, and subjects ships and rivers; built cosmos, released water, and provision meet in one ayah.
Sun and moon run constantly and night and day are subjected, completing the ordered creation-and-provision sequence of 14:32.
Water descends from heaven as drink and as the source of vegetation where animals pasture, joining the section's water-share, field, and herd.
The same rain grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits; it gives the cultivated result opposite the section's barren aftermath.
Night, day, sun, moon, and stars are all subjected by command, setting the ordered cosmic watch immediately beside the watered field of 16:10-11.
Worldly life is rain mingling with earth's growth until God's command comes by night or day and leaves it reaped; it unites water, flourishing field, severing, and the irreversible turn.
Valleys flow according to their measure while the torrent carries swelling foam that vanishes; this makes measured water bear an image of overflow and of what passes versus remains.

Water descends, travels as springs within earth, raises varied crops, then leaves them yellow debris; the whole measured passage from hidden water to growth and waste parallels the section's field movement.

The ayah forbids violating sacred signs and aggression, then pairs cooperation in righteousness and taqwa against sin and transgression; protected animal-boundaries and moral restraint meet explicitly.
A response to aggression must equal the aggression, and the command to practice taqwa follows; restraint and measured return stand together as in the water-share and punishment meeting.
Those who practice taqwa are told that every soul must look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow; inward restraint is joined directly to the consequence following one's act.
Whoever practices taqwa receives a way out, making restraint itself a protecting boundary rather than the breached cover of fujur.
God provides unexpectedly and has set a measure for everything; this completes 65:2 by joining taqwa, provision, and measure.
Had the towns believed and practiced taqwa, blessings from sky and earth would have opened; this is the precise communal reversal of denial turning an ordered, fertile land into destruction.
Thamud deny the messengers, beginning the fuller version of the scene whose messenger, restraint, camel, and punishment follow.
Salih commands his people to practice taqwa; this is the messenger's restraining word directly opposed to the later obedience of transgressors.
Salih identifies himself as a trustworthy messenger, clarifying the divinely commissioned side of the section's messenger versus self-launched culprit contrast.
Salih again commands taqwa and obedience immediately before forbidding obedience to the extravagant in 26:151; the two imperatives mark the opposed authorities.
The arrogant chiefs ask whether the oppressed know that Salih is sent by his Lord, explicitly placing divine sending inside the Thamud confrontation.
The arrogant reject what Salih was sent with, supplying the refusal that moves from the divine mission of 7:75 to the camel's hamstringing in 7:77.
When God's command comes, Salih and the believers are saved while the wrongdoers are left for the blast; protection and communal consequence divide at the appointed turn.
The question "how were My punishment and warnings?" makes the consequence of the self-initiated hamstringing in 54:29 explicit before 54:31 depicts the remains.
God sends Salih to Thamud, who split into two contending groups; divine mission and the community's own divergent movement appear together.
Salih asks why they seek to hasten evil before good and calls them to forgiveness, exposing their self-propelled rush toward the consequence of 27:51.
Earlier peoples are seized because of their sins after their messengers bring clear proofs, completing 40:21's built-earth traces with messenger, denial, and consequence.
Inheritors of ruined lands are warned that God could strike them for their sins; land and the consequence following ذنب meet directly.
Corruption appears on land and sea because of what people's hands earn so that they taste part of what they did; inward breach becomes environmental disorder and measured consequence.
A calamity comes from what people's hands have earned, while much is pardoned; this states the act-to-aftermath relation with an explicit boundary against imagining automatic total requital.
The earth belongs to God, who gives it to whom He wills, and "the outcome is for the muttaqin"; land, taqwa, and aftermath are joined in one promise.
After an unseen community story, the Prophet is told to be patient because "the outcome is for the muttaqin"; restraint governs what comes after.
People are told to travel through the earth and see the deniers' outcome; ruined lands make ʿaqiba a visible trace behind communal denial.
The same travel command directs attention to the deniers' outcome, making destroyed places evidence of what followed their act.
Former peoples cultivated earth and built it more greatly, yet their outcome followed rejection of messengers; this directly joins construction, field, mission, and aftermath.
Travelers are asked to see the outcome of peoples stronger than themselves; vanished power and earthworks illuminate the fate of Thamud's confident architecture.
The command to see former peoples' outcome notes their greater numbers, strength, and traces on earth; their works could not protect them from consequence.
The command to see earlier peoples' outcome states that God destroyed them; the visible ruined-land formulation closely matches the section's leveled houses.
A people who thought their fortresses would protect them have their houses ruined by their own hands and believers' hands; built security becomes the instrument and site of consequence.
Mountains are removed and the earth appears exposed at gathering, supplying a judgment scene in which all raised structures and relief vanish.
Earth and mountains are lifted and crushed in one crushing, a direct large-scale parallel to the section's destructive leveling.
The earth is crushed repeatedly at judgment, extending the section's leveled plain from one people to the final scene.
The question about the mountains is answered by their being blown away; it supplies the object and action whose level-plain result appears in 20:106-107.
Your Lord is ever watchful closes the sequence of transgression, corruption, and poured punishment, reinforcing the section's divine stance beyond fear of any counter-consequence.
Thamud are guided but prefer blindness, so humiliating punishment seizes them for what they earned; wrong choice and its following consequence are stated together.
Believers who practiced taqwa are saved beside Thamud's seizure in 41:17, making restraint the protective opposite of their chosen blindness.
Thamud are granted enjoyment only for a time, giving their prosperity an explicitly measured limit before the blast.
They defy their Lord's command, so the thunderbolt seizes them while they look; broken restraint and immediate consequence meet.
After one man rose to attack the camel, the punished people cannot rise and receive no help; their inability to stand is a pointed reversal of the section's self-launching image.
God leaves nothing of Thamud remaining; the terse statement reinforces the total, unreversed finality developed at the section's close.
God gives Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wrong her; divine giving and human violation are stated together before punishment.
Many towns receive God's might by night or while resting at midday; communal judgment arrives within the same daily alternation that the section turns into a final watch.
The towns are asked whether they feel secure from punishment coming by night while they sleep, making night-cover a possible closure of judgment.
The paired warning asks whether punishment may come in morning brightness while they play; night and morning alike remain appointed turns under divine rule.
Lot is told that his people's fixed appointment is morning and that morning is near; the divinely fixed turn illustrates a judgment no human can delay or reverse.
A settled punishment reaches Lot's people in the early morning, another specific scene in which the ordinary night-day turn becomes terminal judgment.
